| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the cross-platform persistence the stealer installs while disguised as Node tooling: Windows staging under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, macOS LaunchAgent com.nvm.protocal.plist, and Linux systemd user service nvmconf.service. Article-specific because these exact persistence names are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-unique persistence names from the article (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service) — the misspelled 'protocal' and 'nvmconf' are distinctive enough that a hit is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally writing to C:\ProgramData\NodePackages (verify against the exact plist/service names)
  • Restored backup re-creating a previously-quarantined persistence file
  • IR responder copying the artifact for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the persistence file content points to a NodePackages-staged payload or beacon; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: remove the LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Run entry, kill the persisted process, isolate the host, and rotate all credentials/wallets used there. 3) Hunt: correlate with 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and the easy-day-js install artifacts on the same and peer hosts; sweep all OS types since persistence is cross-platform.

| where FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages" or FileName in~ ("com.nvm.protocal.plist","nvmconf.service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated cross-platform crypto-stealer/RAT second stage by file hash on both write and execution. Hash matching is resilient to IP/infra rotation and is effectively zero-FP; the primary hash (221c45...) is the article-named stage-2 payload corroborated by Microsoft. Rationale: Primary hash 221c45a7... is the article-named second-stage payload and is corroborated by Microsoft Threat Intelligence; the additional campaign hashes are bundled IOCs. Hash matching is zero-FP and survives infrastructure rotation, complementing the IP-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox host where the sample was intentionally executed
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy retaining the hash on disk
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: any hit is high-confidence malicious — confirm host, user, and whether the hash was written vs executed; the payload self-deletes, so a FileWrite without a later process may indicate cleanup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and treat as full credential+wallet compromise — rotate cloud/npm/dev secrets and assume browser-stored wallet data exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and NodePackages/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence; submit the hash to org-wide retro-hunt across EDR.

( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ProcExec", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176

DeviceRegistryEvents

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host making an outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 39.107.60.51 used by 15 trojanized JetBrains Marketplace plugins (DeepSeek/CodeGPT clones) to ship stolen OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys. The connection is initiated by the JetBrains IDE JVM the instant a user clicks Apply on the plugin settings, so the process context is a Java/JetBrains runtime, not a browser. Rationale: Anchored on the single hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 (verbatim from the article's network-call code block, defanged 39.107.60[.]51) — a dedicated attacker host with no legitimate use, cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News. Any connection is dispositive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-ai.html • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/sandbox detonating one of the named plugins to reproduce the IOC
  • Threat-intel or attack-surface scanners (Shodan/Censys) probing the IP from a corporate egress
  • IP reuse: the Alibaba Cloud address later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • A SOAR/enrichment playbook auto-resolving or pinging the IOC and generating an event
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is a JetBrains runtime (idea64.exe/pycharm64.exe/java/jetbrains-runtime) and pull the user; enumerate that user's installed JetBrains plugins against the 15 named IDs. 2) Contain: treat every AI provider API key (OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow) entered on that host as compromised — revoke and rotate immediately, uninstall the plugin, and block 39.107.60.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for the IP, and pivot to UC 'malicious JetBrains plugin install' to find dormant infections that haven't yet phoned home.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName,
          SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL,
          ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the application-layer signature of the theft in web-proxy/network-sensor telemetry: a plaintext HTTP POST to the URI path /api/software/<name> carrying the victim's API key as JSON. This survives C2 IP rotation by keying on the distinctive hardcoded URL path, and catches IDE traffic that egresses through a proxy where EDR socket attribution is weak. Rationale: Uses two verbatim article strings — the URL path /api/software/ from the network-call code block and the C2 IP 39.107.60.51 — over plaintext HTTP (article: 'reached over plain HTTP'). The path keys the detection independently of the IP. Datadog/Falcon left empty: standard FDR network events and the listed Datadog sources don't carry HTTP URI paths, so this needs proxy/web-gateway telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fifteen-jetbrains-marketplace/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal/SaaS API that legitimately exposes a '/api/software/' inventory endpoint reached over HTTP
  • Software-asset-management or patch agents POSTing to a vendor '/api/software/' path
  • Web-app vulnerability scanners fuzzing '/api/' routes from a corporate host
  • Proxy replay/cached events double-counting the same flow
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51" or Url has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full request — confirm the host header/destination resolves to 39.107.60.51 and, if PCAP/full-proxy is available, look for the static header X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing an 'sk-' key. 2) Contain: rotate/revoke the leaked provider key(s), remove the offending JetBrains plugin, and add both the IP and the URI path as egress-block + proxy-deny rules. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for any other host hitting /api/software/ (catches infections after a C2 IP change) and correlate with the endpoint-egress UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/software/" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (Url has "/api/software/" or DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51")
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts on-disk presence or install of any of the 15 trojanized JetBrains plugins by matching their Marketplace display names under a JetBrains \plugins\ directory. Covers the initial-access/supply-chain step and surfaces dormant infections on hosts that haven't yet entered an API key or phoned home to the C2. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim list of 15 malicious plugin display names installed under JetBrains \plugins\ paths — the supply-chain delivery artifact. Hunting-tier because the 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone name overlaps the legitimate CodeGPT plugin, so matches need confirmation (pair with the C2-egress UC). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/ • https://hackread.com/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-deepseek-openai-api-keys/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The legitimate 'CodeGPT' plugin (genuine vendor) whose folder name substring overlaps the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone
  • Developers who installed an affected plugin before JetBrains' takedown and have since updated/removed it (stale on-disk artifact)
  • Security team deliberately installing a sample for analysis in a lab VM
  • JetBrains Marketplace cache/temp extraction folders retaining the plugin name after backend disable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Marketplace\\cache\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact plugin ID inside the matched folder's plugin.xml against the 15 known IDs (e.g. org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit) — this disambiguates the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' from the legitimate CodeGPT. 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin, and immediately revoke/rotate any OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key the developer may have entered (assume compromised even without observed egress). 3) Hunt: pivot every matched host to the C2-egress and HTTP-path UCs for 39.107.60.51 to confirm exfiltration, and query software inventory across the fleet for the remaining plugin IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20)
          by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\chrome.exe'

Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-16 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 discovered a Vertex AI Python SDK vulnerability that allows remote code execution via bucket squatting. Read the article for more. The post Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI model upload to default predictable staging bucket (bucket-squat exposure) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vertex AI model deployment following default-staged upload (poisoned-model deploy) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Foreign / non-Vertex principal accessing Vertex AI staging-bucket objects · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vertex AI model upload to default predictable staging bucket (bucket-squat exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel operations that relied on the SDK's default deterministic staging bucket name ('{project}-vertex-staging-{region}') instead of an explicitly-pinned bucket. Per CVE-2026-2473, any upload using this default pattern is exposed to cross-tenant bucket squatting, so each hit must be checked to confirm the staging bucket is owned by your own project. Rationale: Anchored on the exact deterministic string '-vertex-staging-' from the article's gcs_utils.py snippet ('project + "-vertex-staging-" + location') plus the aiplatform UploadModel method; defender/sentinel/cloudwatch/falcon are empty because this telemetry only exists in GCP Cloud Audit Logs (no canonical Defender/Sentinel/AWS table). Cross-checked CVE and method behaviour against The Hacker News, CSO Online and GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine ML pipeline uploads that intentionally use the default staging bucket already owned and pre-created in your own project
  • Data scientists running ad-hoc aiplatform.Model.upload() during model development
  • CI/CD model promotion jobs that never set staging_bucket explicitly
  • Notebook-driven experimentation where the same default bucket is reused across many uploads
Suppression filter
Refine in Datadog/Splunk by excluding uploads whose staging bucket is confirmed self-owned via a Reference Table of your project's known staging buckets, e.g. Splunk: | search NOT [ inputlookup owned_vertex_staging_buckets | fields bucket ]
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, resolve the staging bucket name '{project}-vertex-staging-{region}' and run 'gsutil ls -L -b gs://<name>' / Storage API to confirm the bucket's owning project == your project. If owned elsewhere, you are squatted. 2) Contain: halt the deployment pipeline, delete/quarantine the uploaded model version, and pin an explicit attacker-proof staging_bucket; verify google-cloud-aiplatform is upgraded to >=1.148.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate all Vertex projects/regions for the same default pattern, check whether any squatted artifacts were already deployed (DeployModel), and review GCS object-access logs on the bucket for foreign principals.
title: Vertex AI Model Upload Using Default Predictable Staging Bucket

Foreign / non-Vertex principal accessing Vertex AI staging-bucket objects AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects GCS object create/delete/get operations on objects living in a '*-vertex-staging-*' bucket performed by a principal that is NOT the Vertex AI service agent (P4SA). This catches the attacker's model-replacement write (poisoning) and model-theft reads against a Vertex staging bucket you control, the core of the Pickle-in-the-Middle race window. Rationale: Targets the 'replace the legitimate model' tamper step and model theft by filtering storage.objects.* on the article's '-vertex-staging-' bucket pattern and excluding the legitimate Vertex P4SA (gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com); GCS data-access audit is GCP-only, hence empty Defender/Sentinel/AWS/Falcon fields. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1530 T1565.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The user or CI service account that performed the model upload writing artifacts into its own staging bucket
  • Backup or lifecycle tooling copying/cleaning objects in the staging bucket
  • A monitoring or DLP scanner doing storage.objects.get across all buckets
  • Terraform/infra automation managing staging bucket contents
Suppression filter
Add an allowlist of expected uploader identities, e.g. Datadog: append ' -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:(your-ml-pipeline-sa@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com)'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal and its source IP/project; determine whether it belongs to your org's IAM and whether it should ever touch staging buckets. Note object names — saved_model.pb, *.pkl, *.joblib being overwritten is high-signal. 2) Contain: revoke the principal's access to the bucket, lock the bucket (remove public/cross-project IAM), and block deployment of any model version staged during the access window. 3) Hunt: pull all DeployModel events that referenced affected artifacts, inspect deployed model artifacts for malicious pickle __reduce__ payloads, and rotate any credentials reachable from the Vertex serving environment.

Vertex AI model deployment following default-staged upload (poisoned-model deploy) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel that used the default '-vertex-staging-' bucket with a subsequent EndpointService.DeployModel in the same project within a short window. Deployment is the moment the staged (potentially attacker-replaced) artifact is loaded and the pickle/joblib payload executes in the serving container, so this is the last victim-visible checkpoint before RCE. Rationale: Pairs the default-staging UploadModel signal with the downstream DeployModel (the article's RCE trigger when joblib.load()/pickle.load() runs in the serving container); Sigma is empty because this is a temporal cross-event correlation, and the bare Datadog query surfaces deploys for rule-level correlation since Datadog cannot express the join inline. GCP-only telemetry, so non-GCP platform fields are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal MLOps flow where upload-then-deploy of a self-owned default-staged model is expected behaviour
  • Automated retraining pipelines that upload and immediately deploy on a schedule
  • Blue/green or canary endpoint rollouts deploying multiple model versions in quick succession
  • A/B experimentation deploying several models to the same endpoint within the window
Suppression filter
Scope the correlation to projects/SAs not on the approved MLOps allowlist, e.g. Splunk: append '| search NOT principal IN ("mlops-deployer@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com")'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the upload's staging bucket is self-owned (see UC1); if ownership is uncertain or external, treat the deployed model as poisoned. 2) Contain: undeploy the model from the endpoint, delete the model version, and isolate/rotate any service-account credentials and secrets accessible from the Vertex serving environment (data exfil / lateral movement risk). 3) Hunt: inspect the deployed artifact for malicious pickle __reduce__ gadgets, review egress from the serving container's project, and sweep all projects for default-staged-then-deployed models on vulnerable SDK (<1.148.0).

| rename data.protoPayload.methodName as method, data.resource.labels.project_id as project, data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail as principal
| transaction project maxspan=60m startswith=eval(method="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel") endswith=eval(method="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.DeployModel")
| search "vertex-staging"
| table _time project principal method eventcount duration

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
